reviewSession.heading: Ethics: objective 1.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 1 together, one objective at a time, starting with ethics. The exam expects the four canons in their exact order: protect society, act honourably and legally, serve your principals, and advance the profession. A principal is your employer or client. People most often mix up who ranks first, because the employer is the one who pays you. Remember that society and the law rank above the employer. When canons clash, the higher canon decides what matters, and a proper written process decides how you act. So the best answer is rarely going public and rarely staying silent. It is raising the matter in writing, pressing for a fix, and using lawful routes if that fails. Also remember who may complain to ISC2. Anyone may complain under the first two canons, principals under the third, and other professionals under the fourth.

reviewSession.heading: The security goals: objective 1.2
reviewSession.body: Next come the five security goals: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity and nonrepudiation. When you read a scenario, ask what actually went wrong. Was something seen, changed, lost, faked or denied? Seen points to confidentiality, changed to integrity, lost to availability, faked to authenticity, and denied to nonrepudiation. Do not be misled by the method. Ransomware uses encryption, but when files are locked, the first goal harmed is availability. The classic mix-up is the digital signature. It gives integrity, authenticity and nonrepudiation, but it does not give confidentiality. Another favourite is the shared account or shared key. Neither can prove which person acted, so neither gives nonrepudiation. Finally, the goals compete with one another. The right balance depends on what the business does, and in any scenario involving lives, safety decides.

reviewSession.heading: Governance: objective 1.3
reviewSession.body: Now governance, which means how leaders direct and oversee an organization. The biggest idea is that security serves the business. If an answer protects things perfectly, but stops the business from working, be suspicious of it. Senior management holds final responsibility and cannot hand it away. If a program has no authority, senior support is the first thing to look for. Keep the roles clear. The data owner decides, the custodian carries out, and the auditor checks independently and does not fix. In acquisitions, assess before you connect. In divestitures, separate access and data cleanly. Match each control framework to its purpose. ISO 27001 is the one you can be certified against. And separate two phrases that people swap all the time. Due diligence is researching, planning and checking. Due care is taking the reasonable action. A wise leader does both and keeps the records to prove it.

reviewSession.heading: Law and compliance: objective 1.4
reviewSession.body: In law and compliance, the exam wants you to know which rule is which, and to involve legal advisers when the answer is unclear. The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is not a law. It is an industry standard enforced by contract, and it is still binding. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, know the controller, who decides why and how data is used, and the processor, who acts for the controller. Know the 72-hour rule for telling the supervisory authority, counted from becoming aware of the breach. Know the four kinds of intellectual property and how long each one lasts. A trade secret lasts as long as it stays secret. For moving data or technology across borders, check first and move afterwards. And remember the trap in export controls: sending technical data over a network can count as an export. Encryption is useful, but it does not settle a legal question.

reviewSession.heading: Investigations: objective 1.5
reviewSession.body: Let us review the five investigation types: administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory and industry standards. The key is to link each type to who leads it and how much proof it needs. Administrative is internal, with the lowest standard. Criminal is led by law enforcement and needs proof beyond a reasonable doubt, which is high, but is not the same as absolute certainty. Civil is a dispute between parties, decided on a preponderance of the evidence, which means more likely than not. For regulatory cases, the standard varies. Industry standards cases get their authority from contract. To tell regulatory from industry standards, ask who holds the authority. People also forget that an internal case can quickly become criminal. So protect evidence from the start and keep a chain of custody. If you find signs of crime, stop, preserve what you found, and go to management and legal advisers. Do not confront the suspect.

reviewSession.heading: Policy documents: objective 1.6
reviewSession.body: Here is a quick pass through the security documents. There are five: policy, standard, baseline, guideline and procedure. Only the guideline is optional. That single fact wins many questions. Now the clues to look for. If a document is high level, says what must be achieved, and is approved by senior management, it is a policy. If it names a product or an exact level, it is a standard. If it lists minimum settings for a type of system, it is a baseline. If it uses words like should or consider, it is a guideline. If it gives numbered steps, it is a procedure. People commonly confuse a policy with a standard, because both are mandatory. A policy never names products. When two documents conflict, the higher one wins and the lower one is corrected. And if staff ignore a rule, first ask whether it was approved, communicated and understood.

reviewSession.heading: Business continuity: objective 1.7
reviewSession.body: Continuity questions often turn on order and on simple arithmetic. Senior management support comes first, then the business impact analysis. That analysis measures impact, and it does not choose solutions. If someone proposes a product during the analysis, they have jumped ahead. Now the time measures. Maximum Tolerable Downtime is the cliff edge. Recovery Time Objective is the target for restoring the system. Work Recovery Time covers testing and catching up. The recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must not be more than the maximum tolerable downtime. So if the downtime limit is 10 hours and catching up takes 4, the longest recovery time objective is 6 hours. Recovery Point Objective is different. It looks backward and measures lost data, so backups must be at least that frequent. Check that outside suppliers can meet your own targets. And in any disaster scenario, people's safety comes before everything else.

reviewSession.heading: People: objective 1.8
reviewSession.body: With personnel security, follow a person's working life from start to finish. Before hiring, match screening to the risk of the job, follow the law and get consent. Before access, get the agreements signed, because a non-disclosure agreement often continues after someone leaves. In daily work, least privilege limits access, and separation of duties splits sensitive tasks. Job rotation and mandatory vacation help uncover fraud, since a second person sees the work. On a transfer, remove the old access, or privilege creep builds up. On a forced termination, disable access at the moment the person is told, or just before. A very common wrong answer is disabling access long before the meeting, or long after it. Treat contractors with the same discipline, and tie their access to the contract end date. Tell people in advance if they are monitored. And whenever a single person's error points to a weak process, fix the process.

reviewSession.heading: Risk management: objective 1.9
reviewSession.body: Risk management carries a lot of weight in this domain. First, the maths. Single loss expectancy equals asset value times exposure factor. Annualized loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence. An event once in 20 years has a rate of 1 divided by 20, or 0.05. A safeguard's value equals the yearly loss before, minus the yearly loss after, minus the yearly cost of the safeguard. Forgetting to subtract that cost is the classic mistake. Next, the responses: mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept. Insurance transfers cost, but not accountability. Ignoring a risk is never valid. Residual risk is what remains after controls, and senior management decides whether to accept it. Security staff advise, but do not decide. Know the control purposes, such as preventive, detective and compensating. And know the seven NIST steps in order: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor.

reviewSession.heading: Threat modeling: objective 1.10
reviewSession.body: For threat modeling, the first thing to remember is timing. Start early, at the design stage, while changes are cheap, and repeat the work whenever the system changes. Then keep the methods apart by what each one does. STRIDE names six kinds of threat: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. DREAD scores threats on five questions, so you can rank them. PASTA is a seven-stage process that begins and ends with business risk. VAST suits agile development at scale. Trike looks at what each person is allowed to do with each asset. Attack trees map the paths to an attacker's goal. A frequent confusion is between spoofing and elevation of privilege. Pretending to be someone else is spoofing. Gaining more power than you should have is elevation of privilege. And remember to look hardest at trust boundaries, where data crosses from a less trusted place into a more trusted one.

reviewSession.heading: Supply chain and awareness: objectives 1.11 and 1.12
reviewSession.body: Now the last two objectives. For the supply chain, always ask who touched this before it reached you. Tampering alters a real product, counterfeits imitate one, and implants hide something inside. Assess suppliers before you sign, and keep monitoring them after. An SLR, or Service Level Requirement, is the need, and an SLA, or Service Level Agreement, is the formal promise. A silicon root of trust checks startup code, a physically unclonable function gives a chip a unique identity, and a software bill of materials lists what is inside software. You can outsource work, but not accountability. For awareness, remember that awareness is what, training is how, and education is why. Champions carry the message into departments. Treat a person who clicks with kind, quick teaching. Review content regularly, including trends such as artificial intelligence. And measure behaviour, because attendance proves very little.

reviewSession.heading: How to choose the best answer
reviewSession.body: Let us finish with how to choose. Exam questions often contain more than one answer that would help. Your job is to pick the best one, so read the small words carefully. FIRST asks about order. BEST and MOST ask you to compare. Now put on your manager's hat. You are an adviser, and you are not the technician on the keyboard. Ask four things. Are people safe? Does this answer fix the cause, or only the symptom? Does it follow policy and the law? And who owns this decision? Very often, the owner is senior management, and your job is to give them clear facts. Be careful with answers that are dramatic, secret or based on one person acting alone. Be careful, too, with a technical purchase offered as a first step. Understand the situation first, assess it, and then act. Calm, lawful and well documented is the pattern to look for in this domain.
